pages.text: A machine with a console can be tuned without its sliders, and set once for many copies.

Strike a $(item)Tuning Fork$() against the machine (on a multiblock, against its controller). It opens a short calibration game that fits the machine's science: most machines match a waveform; telescopes, spectrometers and the optical machines line up a spectrum; reactors, plasma machines, colliders and pumps route a flow through pipe tiles; the chemistry machines balance an equation, write one from the species on hand, give oxidation states or write an equilibrium constant; the logic machines chain a proof. Solve it and the machine is set at a working point for the recipe it is running: it runs, but not at its best. Later machines play harder games. The fork only moves the settings: it gives no coolant. If no setting works with the coolant the machine holds, it says which coolant would.

The console is for the fine work. Its $(thing)precision$() shows how close the settings are to the recipe's ideal point, and it falls off fast. At full precision every cycle makes half as much again of each product. Under $(thing)For 100% precision$(), the console's $(thing)Readout$() lists what the recipe's windows and the speed read at its best point: work out which settings bring the readout there (past a one-sided target is fine), and each line turns green. On older multiblocks, precision is how close the tuning dial sits on its drifting target.
A $(item)Calibration Card$() copies settings. Sneak-use it on a tuned machine, then use it on another of the same kind. It is never used up.

Scroll over a value to change it (with shift, five at a time), or click the arrows at its ends. A wrong answer only says "not yet"; nothing is lost. Older multiblocks without a console have their tuning dial set the same way.
The $(item)Resonant Tuning Fork$() never wears out, and says how far a wrong answer is off.
